notes: Pass rate is 100% in both configurations across all 3 evals (12/12 assertions in with_skill, 13/13 in without_skill) - these assertions do not discriminate with-skill from without-skill performance for a model this capable. This is itself a meaningful finding, not a grading failure: the model consistently reaches for git/decision-history archaeology on its own and converges on the same conclusions the skill would have handed it directly.

The real, consistent signal is efficiency, not correctness: with_skill averaged 1161.9s/250,436 tokens vs without_skill's 1449.3s/291,008 tokens - with_skill was faster and cheaper on all 3 evals (by 21-45% wall-clock time). The skill's main measured value here is pointing directly at already-recorded lessons/history instead of requiring the agent to rediscover them via independent research, not unlocking a qualitatively better answer.

Methodological confound on eval 1 (coastline-gap-triage) specifically: isolation:worktree forked each subagent from a stale/inconsistent base ref rather than the session's actual working branch. The without_skill run for eval 1 landed on an especially old commit (a2b9768, pre-dating the entire geometry-cleanup branch), giving it ~404,600 km2 of gaps vs the with_skill run's ~4,701 km2 on much newer data - a 2-order-of-magnitude difference driven by data vintage, not skill presence. Both agents handled this honestly and disclosed it, but the raw numbers in that one pairing are not comparable.

Shared-scratchpad leakage: the without_skill run for eval 1 incidentally found leftover files (an early skill draft, a diagnose_coastline_gaps.py prototype) from unrelated earlier work in the same session's shared scratchpad directory. It did not treat these as authoritative and verified independently, but this means that particular baseline wasn't perfectly blind to the skill's existence - future iterations should use a clean/isolated scratchpad per run.

Both with_skill runs for evals 1 and 2 produced slightly more specific/actionable output than their baselines despite equal assertion pass rates: eval 1's with_skill run found a genuine blind spot in diagnose_coastline_gaps.py itself (COASTLINE-category cells never get aspect-ratio-checked, only land-only cells do) and discovered a novel along-coast-vs-perpendicular heuristic; eval 2's with_skill run proposed a fix scoped to just Kirkuk (narrower, safer) vs the baseline's whole-Iraq-zone scope. Current binary assertions don't capture this kind of depth/precision difference - worth a rubric dimension in a future iteration if this pattern holds up at larger scale.

No assertions failed in either configuration, so there's no evidence yet of what the skill prevents a baseline from getting wrong outright - a genuinely harder/more adversarial eval design (e.g. a case where the historically-correct answer is NOT already recorded in docs/DECISIONS.md, forcing the agent to reason from the skill's general principles rather than retrieve a specific precedent) would more directly test the skill's generalization value rather than its role as a documentation index.
